description:
Can You Spot Tonight's Secret Lunar Eclipse?

Episode 102 of a daily journey through the universe. 🌕
Tonight, February 20, 2027, the full Moon slides through Earth's faint outer shadow: a penumbral lunar eclipse peaking about 23:12 UTC, best seen from Europe, Africa and Asia, with the Moon rising already in eclipse over the Americas. Why it's so hard to notice, and what to look for.

➡️ Tomorrow, Episode 103: Next stop, rogue black holes. Invisible monsters wandering the galaxy.
Start from Episode 1 "Leaving Earth" on the channel.
Follow so you don't miss a stop. A new episode every day.

segments.text: There's a lunar eclipse tonight, and most people won't even notice. Can you?
Tonight, February twentieth, the full Moon passes through Earth's shadow. But there's a catch.
segments.headline: Tonight: an eclipse

segments.text: Earth's shadow has two parts. A dark inner shadow, the umbra, and a pale outer shadow, the penumbra.
segments.headline: Two shadows

segments.text: Tonight, the Moon only touches the pale one. That's a penumbral eclipse.
Standing on the Moon, you'd see Earth cover only part of the Sun.
segments.headline: The view from the Moon

segments.text: From Earth, the change is very subtle. Look for a faint gray shading on one edge of the Moon.
segments.headline: Look for gray shading

segments.text: The deepest moment is around twenty-three twelve, Universal Time. Europe, Africa and Asia see it best.
In the Americas, the Moon rises with the eclipse already ending. Look east, low, right after sunset.
segments.headline: Americas: look east at moonrise

segments.text: Take a photo with your phone, and another one later. Compare them. Can you see the shadow?
segments.headline: Try the photo test

segments.text: Tomorrow, something far darker. Black holes wandering the galaxy alone, invisible, and one of them was caught. Which part surprised you most? Tell me in the comments, and follow for tomorrow's stop.
